concepts.name: Balance of Payments (BoP): Overall Architecture and Accounting Identity
key_dimensions: Double-entry bookkeeping principle — every transaction has a debit and credit entry, so BoP always 'balances' as an accounting statement
Distinction between BoP as an accounting identity (always zero) vs. BoP 'surplus/deficit' which refers to the overall balance requiring reserve adjustment
IMF Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6) framework adopted by RBI — key changes from BPM5
UPSC trap: 'BoP is always in equilibrium' — true accounting sense vs. false policy sense

concepts.name: Current Account: Structure and Sub-components
key_dimensions: Four sub-components: Merchandise trade (goods), Services trade (invisibles), Primary Income (factor income — wages, investment income), Secondary Income (transfers — remittances, grants)
Distinction between 'Visible' trade (goods — forms Trade Balance) and 'Invisible' trade (services + primary + secondary income)
Current Account Deficit (CAD) vs. Current Account Balance — financing implications and sustainability thresholds (RBI's ~2.5% of GDP comfort zone)
UPSC trap: Remittances appear under Secondary Income (Current Account), NOT Capital Account — a frequently tested misclassification

concepts.name: Trade Balance (Merchandise Trade): Concepts and India-specific Patterns
key_dimensions: Exports recorded as credit (+), Imports as debit (−); Trade Deficit = Imports > Exports
India's structural trade deficit — key import drivers: crude oil, gold, electronic goods; key export strengths: engineering goods, petroleum products, gems & jewellery
Difference between data sources: DGCI&S/DGFT customs data vs. RBI BoP data (timing differences, valuation — FOB for exports, CIF for imports in customs; both FOB in BoP)
UPSC trap: Petroleum products are both a major import (crude) AND a major export (refined products) — net vs. gross figures matter

concepts.name: Services Account (Invisibles — Trade in Services)
key_dimensions: Major categories: Travel, Transportation, Insurance & Financial services, Government services, IT/BPO (Other Business Services) — India's surplus driver
India consistently runs a surplus in services trade — software/IT services, business process outsourcing offset goods deficit partially
GATS Mode 1 (cross-border supply) most relevant to India's IT exports — connection between BoP services data and trade negotiations
UPSC trap: Services surplus does NOT fully offset merchandise deficit in India — net invisibles include primary + secondary income too

concepts.name: Primary Income Account (Factor Income Flows)
key_dimensions: Comprises: compensation of employees (wages earned abroad), investment income (dividends, interest, profits on FDI/FPI/external debt), and rent
India typically runs a deficit in Primary Income — outflows of dividends/interest on foreign investment in India exceed inflows
Distinction: Reinvested earnings on FDI are recorded in Primary Income AND simultaneously in Financial Account (as FDI)
UPSC trap: Interest payments on external debt appear under Primary Income (Current Account), not Capital/Financial Account — confusion with principal repayment which IS in Financial Account

concepts.name: Secondary Income Account (Current Transfers)
key_dimensions: Includes: private remittances, workers' remittances, personal transfers, government grants (non-capital), pension transfers
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances (World Bank data) — significant stabilizing role for CAD and foreign exchange reserves
Distinction between current transfers (Secondary Income — no quid pro quo, consumption-oriented) vs. capital transfers (Capital Account — linked to asset acquisition)
UPSC trap: Foreign aid/grants — if for consumption/budget support → Secondary Income (Current Account); if for capital project (like building a dam) → Capital Account

concepts.name: Capital Account (Narrow Definition under BPM6)
key_dimensions: Under BPM6, Capital Account is a SEPARATE, small account — includes only capital transfers and acquisition/disposal of non-produced, non-financial assets (e.g., patents, land transactions with embassies)
Capital transfers: debt forgiveness, migrants' transfers (assets carried when migrating), investment grants for fixed assets
Pre-BPM6 usage: 'Capital Account' loosely referred to entire non-current account (now called Financial Account) — source of confusion in older Indian texts and some UPSC questions
UPSC trap: RBI and Indian policy documents sometimes use 'Capital Account' to mean Capital + Financial Account combined — context-dependent interpretation is critical

concepts.name: Financial Account: Structure and Components
key_dimensions: Five functional categories: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI/FII), Financial Derivatives, Other Investment (loans, trade credit, currency & deposits), Reserve Assets
Assets vs. Liabilities perspective: Resident acquiring foreign assets = capital outflow (debit); Non-resident acquiring domestic assets = capital inflow (credit)
Net lending (+) vs. Net borrowing (−) concept — Financial Account balance mirrors Current + Capital Account balance (with sign reversal)
UPSC trap: An increase in reserves is a DEBIT in Financial Account (India acquiring foreign assets), not a credit — counterintuitive but critical for BoP identity understanding

concepts.name: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in BoP
key_dimensions: IMF threshold: 10% or more equity ownership confers 'lasting interest' → classified as FDI (below 10% = FPI)
Components recorded: equity capital, reinvested earnings (even if not repatriated — imputed flows), other capital (inter-company loans between related entities)
FDI vs. FPI distinction in BoP context: FDI = stable, long-term, involves managerial control; FPI = volatile, market-driven, no management role
UPSC trap: Reinvested earnings of foreign companies in India are recorded BOTH as outflow in Primary Income (dividend not paid) AND inflow in FDI Financial Account — symmetrical double entry

concepts.name: Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) in BoP
key_dimensions: Includes: equity securities (stocks below 10% threshold), debt securities (government bonds, corporate bonds), money market instruments
FPI is highly volatile — 'hot money' — can cause sudden BoP stress (as seen in 2013 Taper Tantrum, 2022 Fed rate hike cycles)
Distinction between FII (old SEBI terminology, now merged into FPI) and FPI in BoP recording — same economic concept
UPSC trap: American Depository Receipts (ADRs) and Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) issued by Indian companies — classified as FPI inflows (portfolio equity), not FDI

concepts.name: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) and Trade Credits in BoP
key_dimensions: ECBs classified under 'Other Investment — Loans' in Financial Account; principal inflow = credit, repayment = debit; interest = Primary Income debit
Trade Credit (short-term): credit extended by foreign suppliers for imports — recorded under Other Investment; India's large trade credit stock reflects import financing pattern
ECB policy regulated by RBI (all-in-cost ceiling, end-use restrictions, eligible borrowers) — BoP recording is separate from regulatory framework
UPSC trap: ECB interest payments affect Current Account (Primary Income); ECB principal flows affect Financial Account — bifurcated BoP recording of a single instrument

concepts.name: Reserve Assets and Official Reserve Transactions
key_dimensions: Reserve Assets = Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) + Gold + SDRs + Reserve Tranche Position with IMF — recorded as sub-component of Financial Account
Change in reserves = residual/financing item for overall BoP — BoP surplus → reserves increase (debit in Financial Account); BoP deficit → reserves decrease (credit)
RBI intervention in forex market changes reserve assets — sterilized vs. non-sterilized intervention and its BoP vs. monetary policy implications

UPSC trap: SDR allocation by IMF is recorded as BOTH an increase in Reserve Assets (Financial Account asset) AND a liability (Other Investment liability) — net effect on BoP is zero but gross entries exist

concepts.name: Current Account Deficit (CAD): Sustainability, Financing, and Thresholds
key_dimensions: CAD = excess of imports of goods, services, and income over exports — must be financed by Financial Account surplus (capital inflows) or reserve drawdown
Sustainable vs. unsustainable CAD — depends on: whether financed by stable flows (FDI > FPI > debt), productive use of imported capital, export growth trajectory
India-specific thresholds: RBI considers CAD above ~2.5-3% of GDP as a concern; 2012-13 CAD hit ~4.8% of GDP — crisis threshold example
UPSC trap: A country CAN have a Current Account Deficit and still be accumulating reserves IF capital inflows (Financial Account surplus) exceed the CAD — these are independent concepts

concepts.name: BoP Crisis: Mechanics and India's 1991 Experience
key_dimensions: BoP crisis occurs when a country cannot finance its Current Account Deficit through normal capital inflows and must deplete reserves to unsustainable levels
1991 India: combination of Gulf War (remittances ↓, oil prices ↑), fiscal deficit monetization, political uncertainty → reserves fell to ~2 weeks of import cover → IMF loan, gold pledge
Sequencing of crisis: CAD → capital flight → reserve depletion → currency crisis → IMF conditionality → structural adjustment (LPG reforms)
UPSC trap: India's 1991 crisis was a BoP crisis primarily, not just a fiscal crisis — fiscal deficit contributed but the proximate trigger was external sector stress

concepts.name: Errors and Omissions in BoP
key_dimensions: Errors and Omissions (E&O) is a residual balancing item — arises due to data collection gaps, timing differences, unrecorded transactions, and statistical discrepancies
Large or persistent E&O can indicate significant unrecorded capital flows — sometimes used as a proxy indicator for illicit financial flows/capital flight
E&O in India's BoP — RBI publishes it; its sign and magnitude tracked by economists as signal of data quality and potential hawala/informal flows
UPSC trap: E&O does NOT mean the BoP doesn't balance — it is the item that MAKES the BoP balance; it is a confession of measurement imperfection, not an imbalance

concepts.name: Capital Account Convertibility (CAC): Concept and India's Position
key_dimensions: CAC = freedom to convert domestic financial assets into foreign assets and vice versa at market-determined rates — full freedom to move capital across borders
India has FULL Current Account Convertibility (since 1994, Article VIII of IMF) but only PARTIAL Capital Account Convertibility — different rules for residents vs. non-residents, FDI vs. FPI vs. debt
Tarapore Committee I (1997) and II (2006) — preconditions for full CAC: fiscal consolidation, low inflation, strong banking system; India has not yet achieved full CAC
UPSC trap: Current Account Convertibility ≠ Capital Account Convertibility; India accepting Article VIII obligations means current account convertibility only — a classic UPSC confusion point

concepts.name: Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) and Its BoP Implications
key_dimensions: RBI's LRS allows resident individuals to remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year for any permissible current or capital account transaction — blurs current/capital distinction at individual level
LRS outflows recorded in BoP: current account (education, travel, medical) OR financial account (overseas investment, deposits) depending on purpose
Rising LRS outflows post-COVID (overseas travel, foreign equity investment) contributing to current account pressure — TCS (Tax Collected at Source) on LRS introduced in Union Budget 2023
UPSC trap: LRS is a RESIDENT individual scheme — NRI remittances INTO India are separate (FCNR, NRE accounts) and appear as capital/financial account inflows, not LRS

concepts.name: Twin Deficit Hypothesis and BoP Linkage
key_dimensions: Twin Deficit = Fiscal Deficit + Current Account Deficit occurring simultaneously — Keynesian identity: (G-T) = (S-I) + (M-X); fiscal deficit can crowd out or spill into CAD
Mechanism: High fiscal deficit → government borrowing → higher interest rates → capital inflows → currency appreciation OR fiscal deficit → excess domestic demand → more imports → CAD

India's experience: Not always a strict twin deficit relationship — capital flows, savings rate, and oil prices are independent variables; 2020-21 saw fiscal deficit surge but CAD narrowed (COVID crushed imports)
UPSC trap: Twin deficit is a tendency/hypothesis, NOT an accounting identity — it can be broken (fiscal deficit without CAD or vice versa), and UPSC has asked about exceptions

concepts.name: Marshall-Lerner Condition and J-Curve Effect in BoP Context
key_dimensions: Marshall-Lerner Condition: Currency depreciation improves trade balance (Current Account) ONLY IF sum of price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds 1 (|PEDx| + |PEDm| > 1)

J-Curve Effect: In the short run, depreciation WORSENS trade balance before improving it — because import/export volumes are sticky (contracts, habit), but prices adjust immediately raising import bill
India-specific: Rupee depreciation may not immediately help trade balance because India's exports have low price elasticity (commodities, IT services priced in USD) and oil imports are inelastic
UPSC trap: Depreciation does NOT automatically improve BoP — Marshall-Lerner must hold AND J-curve lag must be weathered; UPSC tests whether students know the conditions, not just the direction

concepts.name: International Investment Position (IIP) and its Relationship with BoP
key_dimensions: IIP is a STOCK concept (snapshot of a country's foreign assets vs. foreign liabilities at a point in time); BoP is a FLOW concept (transactions over a period)
Relationship: Change in IIP = BoP Financial Account flows + valuation changes (exchange rate, price changes) + other adjustments — BoP flows are only ONE reason IIP changes
Net IIP: If liabilities > assets → Net Debtor nation (India is a net debtor); if assets > liabilities → Net Creditor (China, Japan are net creditors)
UPSC trap: A country can have BoP surplus (accumulating reserves) yet remain a net IIP debtor if historical liability stock is large — flow improvement doesn't instantly change stock position
